newsitem.title: UK: UK pension funds earn 3.9 pct in Q197 - WM Company.
newsitem.headline: UK pension funds earn 3.9 pct in Q197 - WM Company.

text.p: UK pension funds made average returns of 3.9 percent in the first quarter of this year, helped by strong performances of overseas equities, a survey by consultants and actuaries WM Company showed on Thursday.
Pension funds enjoyed a 5.2 percent first quarter return on overseas equity holdings, outpacing the 4.2 percent return on the FT/S&P World ex UK index.

But a return of 4.6 percent on UK equities failed to match the FTSE All-Share, which was up 5.3 percent for the quarter. UK equities, at 52.9 percent, are by far the largest holdings of pension funds.

"Funds suffered in the first quarter because of their higher exposure to mid cap stocks at the expense of the better performing companies in the FTSE 100," said Gordon Bagot, a director at WM Company.
"In particular, they had relatively light exposure to some of the quarter's top performing major stocks, including HSBC, BSkyB, SmithKline Beecham and Glaxo."
Larger funds are likely to have performed better in the first quarter because their holdings tend to reflect the composition of the FTSE All-Share more closely than the average, Bagot said.

European shares, not including the UK, were the best performing single asset class in the quarter, registering a gain of 10.8 percent, though funds could not match the 11.2 percent of the FT/S&P Europe ex UK index.

"The outperformance overseas was largely due to significant overweighting in European markets. The outperformance would have been even greater if the pound had not appreciated by almost five percent relative to the main European currencies," Bagot said.
Pension funds made few changes in their asset allocations in the quarter, the survey showed.
A move to European equities was noted, now comprising 9.1 percent of the whole versus 8.5 percent at the end of 1996.

UK pension funds continue to be extremely underweight in US equities, which remain at 3.7 percent of total assets. "Managers are wary of US market valuations," Bagot said, and are reluctant to buy in having missed much of US bull market.
There was little sign of a move to UK gilts, which ticked up to 6.2 percent in the quarter from 6.0 percent at the end of 1996.
The survey covered 75 percent of all UK pension funds.
